task: This is a synthetic exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes as the fixed record: select, organize and phrase the story without inventing additional reported events, scenes, quotations or reporting activity. Write a headline and a reported feature of roughly 450–650 words in AP style for general newspaper readers about the test-shard archive at the Clay Window community pottery studio. Write from this reporting snapshot as of September 18, 2026.

facts.text: The fictional Clay Window studio keeps labeled glaze tests and selected broken pieces beside its communal worktables rather than displaying only finished pots.
Studio technician Hara Venn links each retained test to notes about its clay, glaze and firing batch when those details are known.
The supplied scene describes a beginner comparing a dull green test tile with a glossy sample while the technician looks up their different batch notes.
The archive's purpose is to support comparison and discussion, not guarantee that repeating a label will produce an identical object.
Some older pieces lack complete notes and are marked as incomplete records rather than assigned invented firing information.
Venn said, "The piece that went wrong can be the one people spend longest looking at, provided we know enough to ask a useful question."
The studio began the archive after instructors found themselves describing the same past experiments without being able to show them.
Members can contribute a test or failed piece, but the technician selects what can be stored and documented within the available shelf space.
The studio does not retain every member's work or require anyone to display a personal piece they would prefer to take home.
Member Dera Cole keeps a cracked bowl as a reference for a later version rather than treating it as a finished exhibition piece.
Cole said, "I remember being annoyed with it. Now I can point to the part I changed instead of pretending the next bowl arrived from nowhere."
Kiln operation is handled by designated trained staff under the studio's own procedures, not assigned to any visitor who studies a test tile.
The labels are learning records and do not certify that a glaze or finished pot is suitable for every food or household use.
The packet contains no laboratory safety test or evidence of a measured improvement in every member's work.
The studio charges ordinary membership and class fees, while access to the reference shelves is included for current users of the workspace.
Several metal biscuit tins hold small fragments, with written indexes showing where particular tests have been stored.
Photographs are being added so a record remains available when a fragile piece can no longer be handled.
A photograph can show an appearance but does not preserve the weight and texture that users compare when holding a physical sample.
The studio is planning a small public display about experimentation, with member permission required for named personal work.
The display's date and final selection have not been announced.
The archive includes ordinary repeated tests as well as striking failures, giving users comparisons beyond the most visually dramatic pieces.
The studio has not described the archive as a collection representing all local ceramic traditions.

forbidden_additions: Invented missing batch details or guaranteed reproducible results.
Food-safety certification, laboratory findings or measured universal learning gains.
Unapproved display of named personal work or unrestricted kiln operation.
preserve: The role of imperfect objects and documented comparisons in the shared studio.
Differences between an example, a record and a certification.
Exact quotation wording and attribution when quotations are used.
